Hi.

On Mon, Sep 29, 2008 at 1:44 AM, nongnone <anunc...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Pls explain more in detail about this information, I need to know what
> the meaning in each column.
>
> sample  chromosome      start   stop    mean    count   url
> 840RT0001-20080311-GWS5 1       5130    3138368 -0.014  431
> http://genome.ucsc.edu/cgi-bin/hgTracks?clade=vertebrate&org=Human&db=hg18&position=chr1%3A0-3451692

Please provide code and sessionInfo() showing how you generated that
"information".  I assume you refer to a regions file generated by one
of the segmentation models.  But basically, each row is a region as
identified by the segmentation method.  The columns are:

sample: The name of the sample containing the region.
chromosome, start, stop:  The chromosome and the start and stop
positions (nucleotide position starting at postion 1) of the region.
mean: The mean raw CN of all loci in the region.  (This is typically
the mean of the log2 ratios.)
count: The number of loci (at which there are data points) in the region.
url: A URL to the UCSC Genome Browser showing thethe region +/- some
margins.  This is hardwired to the human genome and current hg18.
There is no easy way to change the latter right now and only there for
your convenience, if it applies.

Cheers

/Henrik

>
>
> Best regards,
> Anunchai Assawamakin
> >
>

>> source("http://www.braju.com/R/hbLite.R")
> Error in file(file, "r", encoding = encoding) :

>  cannot open: HTTP status was '503 Service Unavailable'
>
> I use R 2.7.2 and have installed several bioconductor packages using
> the "source-install" method sucessfully. I am also behind a corporate
> firewall and am generally able to access outside networks fine through
> a proxy server. Any ideas what is going on here?

I don't know, but either it was a one-time failure at the webserver
(but they are rare) or more likely some issue with your firewall/proxy
settings.  It is also not clear what you mean by 'the "source-install"
method'.  For troubleshooting, I'd suggest to:

* Try to connect to http://www.braju.com/R/hbLite.R in a web browser.
* Try to connect to http://www.braju.com/R/hbLite.R using 'wget' (your
on Linux so you probably have this one).
* Try to connect to http://www.braju.com/R/hbLite.R using
download.file("http://www.braju.com/R/hbLite.R") inside R.
* Try do source("http://www.bioconductor.org/biocLite.R").  If that
works, but not source("http://www.braju.com/R/hbLite.R"), then there
is something in your firewall that give you permission to access the
former but not the latter.
* Talk to your corporate's sysadm.

Cheers

/Henrik

On Sep 19, 10:10 pm, "Henrik Bengtsson" <h...@stat.berkeley.edu>
wrote:
> Hi.

>
> On Fri, Sep 19, 2008 at 4:35 AM, marco <mazu.c...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> > Dear List,
>
> >  I wonder about how X chromosome is treated in aroma.affymetrix.
> > Is the mix of male/female samples somehow taken into account, or X is
> > processed as any other chromosome?
>
> Good idea ;)   Yes, the CRMA model does take into account the fact
> that different samples have different ploidies on ChrX when using the
> pool of arrays as a reference.  The idea is to calculate the robust
> average across all arrays and correct for the bias that
> non-copy-neutral samples introduce.   See Section '3.2.7 Reference
> signals' in:
>
> H. Bengtsson; R. Irizarry; B. Carvalho; T. Speed, Estimation and
> assessment of raw copy numbers at the single locus level,
> Bioinformatics, 2008. [pmid: 18204055] [doi:
> 10.1093/bioinformatics/btn016]
>
> for more details.  The model/method requires that at least one sample
> is copy neutral, i.e. you need at least one "female" in order to
> estimate a diploid reference on ChrX.   The same bias-correction
> method can also be used when some of samples are say trisomy 21.   For
> ChrY, our current model cannot give you a *diploid* ChrY reference,
> but a *copy neutral* one, i.e. CN=1 (requires at least one "male").
> To the best of my understand, none of the other methods out there use
> this, but instead it is common to see that only female samples are
> used for the ChrX reference.  See the above CRMA paper to see how much
> the ChrX CN estimates are improved when you use the above
> bias-corrected method instead.
>
>
>
> > In these case the female and males test array are supposed to have
> > log2 values on the average over and below zero?
>
> I'm note sure what you mean by this, but maybe the above answered this
> question too.
>
> So, how do you do this in aroma.affymetrix?  I have on purpose avoided
> giving the details on this until someone asks for it, because it
> involved the use of a new kind of non-finalized sample annotation
> files (SAFs).  I don't want to bother people with alpha versions in
> case the API/format changes.  It is unlikely that it will change much
> but if you can accept that it might change, I created a new vignette
> explaining how to do it:
>

> Vignette 'Sex-chromosome bias-corrected reference signals from pooled average'http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/sex-chromosome-bi...

>
> It also illustrated a lot of other things so it might be useful for others too.
>
> Hope this helps
>
> Henrik
>
>
>
> > Regards
>
> > Marco

messages.subject: Afffy 6.0 using Nsp I only
messages.body_plain:
Dear List:

One of my collaborators wants to do the arrays using NspI only.  It
seems like a reasonable idea since only a small fraction of the
probesets are queried by StyI alone.  Can aroma.affymetrix be used to
analyze such arrays or does it implicitly use that the fragments come
from a mixture of StyI and NspI processed DNA?  Also can the probesets
queried by StyI alone be removed from the precessing (from
normalization down all the steps that follow).

Thanks,
Venkat

messages.subject: Re: Afffy 6.0 using Nsp I only
messages.body_plain:
Hi Venkat,

As far as I am aware, when you buy 6.0 arrays, you get both Nsp and
Sty arrays (http://www.affymetrix.com/products/arrays/specific/
genome_wide_snp6/genome_wide_snp_6.affx), so it would seem odd to
choose not to use a particular array (that you have already
purchased).  This is different from the *500K* arrays where you can
specifically purchase arrays just for Nsp *or* Sty (http://
www.affymetrix.com/products/arrays/specific/500k.affx <http://www.affymetrix.com/products/arrays/specific/500k.affx>).  If your
collaborator chooses to use the 500K arrays, and chooses to use just
Nsp, then that is fine, aroma.affymetrix can analyse arrays from just
a particular enzyme.  See this page:
http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/total-copy-number-analysis?hl=en
for details.

cheers

Lavinia.

Hi Lavinia:

Unlike the 500k array, Affy 6.0 (and 5.0) are single chips.  Different aliquots of DNA are processed by StyI and NspI separately and mixed together and hybed to a single chip. There are reasons why my collaborator wants to use NspI only.

Venkat

>>
>> Good idea ;)   Yes, the CRMA model does take into account the fact
>> that different samples have different ploidies on ChrX when using the
>> pool of arrays as a reference.  The idea is to calculate the robust
>> average across all arrays and correct for the bias that
>> non-copy-neutral samples introduce.   See Section '3.2.7 Reference
>> signals' in:
>>
>> H. Bengtsson; R. Irizarry; B. Carvalho; T. Speed, Estimation and
>> assessment of raw copy numbers at the single locus level,
>> Bioinformatics, 2008. [pmid: 18204055] [doi:
>> 10.1093/bioinformatics/btn016]
>>
>> for more details.  The model/method requires that at least one sample
>> is copy neutral, i.e. you need at least one "female" in order to
>> estimate a diploid reference on ChrX.   The same bias-correction
>> method can also be used when some of samples are say trisomy 21.   For
>> ChrY, our current model cannot give you a *diploid* ChrY reference,
>> but a *copy neutral* one, i.e. CN=1 (requires at least one "male").
>> To the best of my understand, none of the other methods out there use
>> this, but instead it is common to see that only female samples are
>> used for the ChrX reference.  See the above CRMA paper to see how much
>> the ChrX CN estimates are improved when you use the above
>> bias-corrected method instead.
>>
>>
>>
>> > In these case the female and males test array are supposed to have
>> > log2 values on the average over and below zero?
>>
>> I'm note sure what you mean by this, but maybe the above answered this
>> question too.
>>
>> So, how do you do this in aroma.affymetrix?  I have on purpose avoided
>> giving the details on this until someone asks for it, because it
>> involved the use of a new kind of non-finalized sample annotation
>> files (SAFs).  I don't want to bother people with alpha versions in
>> case the API/format changes.  It is unlikely that it will change much
>> but if you can accept that it might change, I created a new vignette
>> explaining how to do it:

>> Vignette 'Sex-chromosome bias-corrected reference signals from pooled average'http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/sex-chromosome-bi...
>>
>> It also illustrated a lot of other things so it might be useful for others too.
>>
>> Hope this helps
>>
>> Henrik
>>
>>

>>

messages.subject: Re: [aroma.affymetrix] Re: Afffy 6.0 using Nsp I only
messages.subject_clean: [aroma.affymetrix] Re: Afffy 6.0 using Nsp I only
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

yes by only hybridizing NspI targets you "only" miss about 160,000
SNPs on GWS6, since all CN probes are designed for NspI and several of
the SNPs designed for StyI are by chance also on the NspI fragments as
well.  So, it makes sense to try this idea out.  I guess except from
the obvious of saving some money on not purchasing the StyI kit, the
main advantage is probably that you save a few hours (days?) of work
in each batch.

You will be able to process the data "as is" through the
aroma.affymetrix pipeline.  You can even use the same annotation files
etc.  Of course, the question is what the result will be.  The
crosstalk calibration should be fine and so the summarization.  The
fragment-length normalization will treat the data as if you hybridized
StyI target as well - the StyI-only signals should be close to zero
(whatever that is) and the model will be fitted to this.  I cannot see
why the current model shouldn't still work, but I might have overseen
something.

One could also consider extending the model where one filter out
certain probes (here StyI probes).  Filtering of probes have been
requested before and it is on the todo list (not very high up though).
 Then, with some modifications to the fragment-length
model/algorithm/implementation, an NspI-only GWS5/6 data set would
effectively be processed as if it was a (more dense) Mapping250K_Nsp
chip.

I'd say, if you already have the data, give the current setup a try
and see if you get decent results.  Any modifications will only get
better from there.  One warning though: If you one day decide to
hybridize with both enzymes, I doubt that you can easily mix the CEL
files from NspI-only and NspI+StyI hybs.  The reference signals
(theta_R) will probably not be comparible, especially not for the
probes target by both enzymes.

I would be interested in looking at this kind of data for another
reason - I'm comparing the different generations of Affymetrix chips
and this data could bring some more understanding to the overall
picture.

Cheers

Henrik

> aliquots of DNA are processed by StyI and NspI separately and mixed together

> use NspI only.

messages.subject: GcRmaBackground Correction
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Sorry to be flogging a dead horse a little, but I thought I'd ask in
case it's an easy fix. I'm trying to run GcRmaBackground correction on
some Human Exon 1.0 ST Arrays. I've converted the "unsupported" Affy cdf
to binary and was using that for the background correcting & quantile
normalising stages, and was planning on switching to a custom cdf for
the PLM fitting.

I heard from some people in an earlier request that you can't do GCRMA
on Exon arrays, but conceptually I'm struggling to see why not, as long
as type="affinities" is used, and the appropriate set of probes is
designated as the MM probes. From the looks of the output I received, it
seems that it uses the non-PM probes as the default MM probes. If there
is an obvious reason why GCRMA shouldn't work, then I'd love to be put
right as well.

Obviously RMA is fine & works very well, but if this can be worked out
easily I figure a few others might benefit. As well as the main
analysis, I'm planning on eventually using the transcript level
estimates for a meta-analysis. The other datasets are all from HG-U133A
arrays processed with GCRMA & I'd like to keep the processing protocols
for all datasets as similar as possible, so as to minimise any effects
related to the processing steps.

Unfortunately the programming for aroma.affymetrix is a bit too
sophisticated for me to try & nut this one out myself. From the looks of
the output I thought it may be a programming issue rather than a "this
is a stupid thing to be trying" issue.

Thanks in advance,

Steve

Here's the code & relevant output:

> >> Good idea ;)   Yes, the CRMA model does take into account the fact
> >> that different samples have different ploidies on ChrX when using the
> >> pool of arrays as a reference.  The idea is to calculate the robust
> >> average across all arrays and correct for the bias that
> >> non-copy-neutral samples introduce.   See Section '3.2.7 Reference
> >> signals' in:
>
> >> H. Bengtsson; R. Irizarry; B. Carvalho; T. Speed, Estimation and
> >> assessment of raw copy numbers at the single locus level,
> >> Bioinformatics, 2008. [pmid: 18204055] [doi:
> >> 10.1093/bioinformatics/btn016]
>
> >> for more details.  The model/method requires that at least one sample
> >> is copy neutral, i.e. you need at least one "female" in order to
> >> estimate a diploid reference on ChrX.   The same bias-correction
> >> method can also be used when some of samples are say trisomy 21.   For
> >> ChrY, our current model cannot give you a *diploid* ChrY reference,
> >> but a *copy neutral* one, i.e. CN=1 (requires at least one "male").
> >> To the best of my understand, none of the other methods out there use
> >> this, but instead it is common to see that only female samples are
> >> used for the ChrX reference.  See the above CRMA paper to see how much
> >> the ChrX CN estimates are improved when you use the above
> >> bias-corrected method instead.
>
> >> > In these case the female and males test array are supposed to have
> >> > log2 values on the average over and below zero?
>
> >> I'm note sure what you mean by this, but maybe the above answered this
> >> question too.
>
> >> So, how do you do this in aroma.affymetrix?  I have on purpose avoided
> >> giving the details on this until someone asks for it, because it
> >> involved the use of a new kind of non-finalized sample annotation
> >> files (SAFs).  I don't want to bother people with alpha versions in
> >> case the API/format changes.  It is unlikely that it will change much
> >> but if you can accept that it might change, I created a new vignette
> >> explaining how to do it:
>
> >> Vignette 'Sex-chromosome bias-corrected reference signals from pooled average'http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/sex-chromosome-bi...
>
> >> It also illustrated a lot of other things so it might be useful for others too.
>
> >> Hope this helps
>
> >> Henrik
>
> >> > Regards
>
> >> > Marco

I see.  For now, you can access the UFL data using
ufl[units,fragments], e.g. ufl[units,2], which returns a data frame.
The rows are indices as units in a CDF (as always in
aroma.affymetrix). There is a developers page on UFL files giving a
hint on this usage:

  http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/unit-fragment-length-ufl-files

The UGP and UFL formats/APIs are still "under development", which is
why I don't announce them more.

Henrik

>> >> Good idea ;)   Yes, the CRMA model does take into account the fact
>> >> that different samples have different ploidies on ChrX when using the
>> >> pool of arrays as a reference.  The idea is to calculate the robust
>> >> average across all arrays and correct for the bias that
>> >> non-copy-neutral samples introduce.   See Section '3.2.7 Reference
>> >> signals' in:
>>
>> >> H. Bengtsson; R. Irizarry; B. Carvalho; T. Speed, Estimation and
>> >> assessment of raw copy numbers at the single locus level,
>> >> Bioinformatics, 2008. [pmid: 18204055] [doi:
>> >> 10.1093/bioinformatics/btn016]
>>
>> >> for more details.  The model/method requires that at least one sample
>> >> is copy neutral, i.e. you need at least one "female" in order to
>> >> estimate a diploid reference on ChrX.   The same bias-correction
>> >> method can also be used when some of samples are say trisomy 21.   For
>> >> ChrY, our current model cannot give you a *diploid* ChrY reference,
>> >> but a *copy neutral* one, i.e. CN=1 (requires at least one "male").
>> >> To the best of my understand, none of the other methods out there use
>> >> this, but instead it is common to see that only female samples are
>> >> used for the ChrX reference.  See the above CRMA paper to see how much
>> >> the ChrX CN estimates are improved when you use the above
>> >> bias-corrected method instead.
>>
>> >> > In these case the female and males test array are supposed to have
>> >> > log2 values on the average over and below zero?
>>
>> >> I'm note sure what you mean by this, but maybe the above answered this
>> >> question too.
>>
>> >> So, how do you do this in aroma.affymetrix?  I have on purpose avoided
>> >> giving the details on this until someone asks for it, because it
>> >> involved the use of a new kind of non-finalized sample annotation
>> >> files (SAFs).  I don't want to bother people with alpha versions in

>> >> but if you can accept that it might change, I created a new vignette
>> >> explaining how to do it:
>>

>>
>> >> It also illustrated a lot of other things so it might be useful for others too.
>>
>> >> Hope this helps
>>
>> >> Henrik
>>
>> >> > Regards
>>

Yes, you can update the footer using readFooter(), update the list
structure, and use writeFooter() to write it back.

I'm not sure I understand where you are heading.  Is your next step to
update the UFL file such that all StyI length are NAs?  If so, it may
or may not work out of the box, but lets see; if not, it is a good
test for now.

I think an slightly different and better approach of what you doing is
to stick with chip type name 'GenomeWideSNP_6' and append the
additional tag 'NspI-only' in addition to the existing 'Full' tag.
This way you would keep all your annotation files for the identical
chip type under the same path, i.e.
annotationData/chipTypes/GenomeWideSNP_6/.   Note that I try to stick
to the definition of a chip type as something that never changes after
the chip is produced in the factory - the probes will always be the
same for GWS6 - it is only the annotation that gets updated.   This is
along the lines what others did with the exon array - there are a few
custom made CDF, but the all live in the same chip type directory.
This way you will also be able to reuse the existing CDF (and UGP).
So, if you are only creating a custom UFL, then do name it as:

annotationData/chipTypes/GenomeWideSNP_6/
   GenomeWideSNP_6,Full,na24,HB20080214,VS20081009,NspI-only.ufl

or similar.  You can update the footer with comments of what you've done.

Does this make more sense?

However, I'd say, if you already have the data, make sure to give the
existing pipeline a try and treat it as there are StyI fragments as
well.  *I think* that CRMA will treat it only as weak signals, but it
won't introduce bias (just a bit of noise).

Cheers

> is a stupid thing to be trying" issue.

To the best of my understanding there is nothing in the gcRMA model
that say it could be applied to any kind of chip type including exon
arrays.   I think it comes down to the algorithm and the
implementation of it.  But again, I am not on top of it and my memory
vanish quickly.

Note, "back in" 2006, Ken Simpson (then at WEHI, Melbourne) ported the
gcRMA steps to aroma.affymetrix.  This was mostly done by adopting and
cut'n'pasting functions from the gcrma package.  A few bells and
whistles has been added such as exception handling and verbose output
and I did some memory optimization, but the main structure of the
algorithm is as in the gcrma package.  I have looked at the gcrma
code/algorithm at times and I recall that it is rather hardwired to
the old expression arrays.  For instance, I think it assumes paired
PMs and MMs etc, but I might be wrong as it is not well documented/few
comments.

>From your log below, it is clear that the current issue "you" have is
to compute the affinities.  This is done only based on the CDF and is
unrelated to the observed signals (CEL files).  The function is done
by the computeAffinities() for AffymetrixCdfFile.  Thus, to start
troubleshooting/narrow down the problem, one can start from:

library("aroma.affymetrix");
verbose <- Arguments$getVerbose(-20, timestamp=TRUE);
cdf <- AffymetrixCdfFile$byChipType("HuEx-1_0-st-v2");
computeAffinities(cdf, verbose=verbose);

FYI, there is also a computeAffinities2() method that is not used, but
when I look at the code and comments, it is clear that I started to
improve/robustify computeAffinities().  The new version is not used
anywhere, but it might be start, if you really want to solve this.

FYI2, if you follow the code you'll find that the issue you observe is
independent of what you set argument 'type' to.  See
print(bgAdjustGcrma.AffymetrixCelSet) as a start.

I'm not using gcRMA correction myself, hence the low priority from my
side.  If you look in the Bioconductor mailinglist archive, you'll
find that there over the last months/half a year has been some issued
raised on (the implementation/algorithm of) gcRMA.

Hope this helps a bit

Henrik

>> misunderstood you or vice versa.
>
> I was trying to avoid the problem of mixing of CEL files using NspI-
> only with those from NspI+StyI hybs.  I believe I misunderstood your
> comment that the reference signals not being comparable.  My mistake
> is probably believing that analyzing the two kinds of CEL files using
> the same annotation data can cause problems.  Will I be OK as long as
> I keep them in separate rawData branches?

Yes, keeping them as separate data sets will lower the risk for mixing
them up.  It is easier to process them independently of each other and
if decide you want to give it a try to process them together, you can
always merge them in the code.  For instance, by doing:

csR <- AffymetrixCelSet$byName("foo", cdf=cdf);
csR2 <- AffymetrixCelSet$byName("bar", cdf=cdf);
append(csR, csR2);
rm(csR2);

the 'csR' object will contain the foo files with the bar files
appended at the end.  The (output) name of what you process with csR
will be decided by the first file in the csR set (this is always the
case for any data set).  By adding a tag in the first processing step
you can separate the merged data sets from the non-merge one, e.g.

qn <- QuantileNormalization(csR, tags="bar,*")

/Henrik

> at a future point.

messages.subject: Re: How to extract all CNs?
messages.body_plain:
[replying to mailing list]

Hi,

On Mon, Oct 13, 2008 at 9:16 AM, Venkatraman E. Seshan
> Hi Henrik:
>
> The affy-GWS6-NspI only cel files were processed with no error messages.
>  The extractRawCopyNumbers complained about log2 of NaNs but I believe that
> was to be expected.  The plot of the raw copy numbers of chromosome 1 of
> array 1 looked fine.

Sounds good.

Yes, with CRMA preprocessing and especially allelic-crosstalk
calibration you'll get non-positive probe signals of which some carry
through to generate non-positive chip-effect estimates.  Non-logged
CNs, C := 2*theta/thetaR, are still valid (rank invariant) though.

>
> Now I want to extract all the raw copy number data into a data frame.
> extractRawCopyNumbers seems to accept 1 array and 1 chromosome at a time.
>  Is there a way I can extract it all in one swoop.

Not sure what you mean by "all" here, since there are two kinds of
"all": all units and all arrays.

The extractRawCopyNumbers() is designed specifically to work with only
one array and one chromosome at the time [it was developed to be an
internal command but there many request for similar features so I made
it public].

If you are happy to calculate your own CN ratios and reference
signals, then the most convenient way is to extract the summarized
signals (chip effects/theta:s) and take it from there.

Say you have a CnChipEffectSet named 'cesN'.  Then, you can extract
the chip-effect estimates across all arrays as:

theta <- extractTheta(cesN, units=units, drop=TRUE);

where 'units' is an index vector (as indexed by the CDF) or NULL to
get all units.  Returned 'theta': The first dimension is always the
unit indices (according to the CDF), and the last is always the array
indices.  If you fit total signals, the the middle dimension is
singular and will be dropped, but if you fit allele-specific signals,
then it is the allele indices, e.g. "A" and "B".

To get the thetas from a specific array, do:

ce <- getFile(cesN, 3)
theta <- extractTheta(ce, units=units, drop=TRUE);

If you do allele-specific estimates and find your self adding
theta=thetaA+thetaB all the time, then there is also:

data <- extractTotalAndFreqB(ce, units=units);

which returns a matrix where the total chip effect,
theta=thetaA+thetaB, is in the 1st column, and the freqB=thetaB/theta
in the 2nd.  For non-SNP units, the freqB estimate is NA.  Except for
some rare cases, this transform is bijective.  If you think about it,
this is a quite generic format, because all chip types/units/platforms
(Affymetrix, Illumina, Agilent, ...) have 'theta' but only the
SNP-specific ones have 'freqB'; if you're only interested in total CN
estimates, you can stick to the first
column.  Analogously, the same method exists for the 'cesN' *set*.

There is also the generic lower-level extractMatrix() method as well
as extractDataFrame(..., addNames=TRUE/FALSE), which returns matrices
where allele A and allele B signals are on separate rows and therefore
somewhat harder to identify/extract if you have mixed SNPs and CN
units.  I recommend to use extractTheta()/extractTotalAndFreqB()
whenever possible.

Hope this helps

Henrik

>
> Thanks,
> Venkat

messages.body_plain:
To get the plotImage commands to work I had to first install
ImageMagick (http://www.imagemagick.org/script/binary-
releases.php#windows), then GTK+ (http://sourceforge.net/projects/gtk-
win/) and finally GPL Ghostscript (http://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~ghost/doc/
GPL/index.htm). Restart windows and start R and load the EBImage
library (library(EBImage)) to confirm that it is working.

Finally in the QC documentation the command:

plotImage(cf, transform=log2, palette=rainbow(256))

does not work. However, changing it to the following seemed to solve
the problem:

plotImage(cf, transform=list(log2), palette=rainbow(256))

Hi,

On Thu, Oct 16, 2008 at 12:19 PM, pwhiteusa <pwhi...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> To get the plotImage commands to work I had to first install

> releases.php#windows), then GTK+ (http://sourceforge.net/projects/gtk-
> win/) and finally GPL Ghostscript (http://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~ghost/doc/
> GPL/index.htm). Restart windows and start R and load the EBImage
> library (library(EBImage)) to confirm that it is working.

yes, installing EBImage requires some setup of additional software,
especially on Windows.  I've documented this on the "Installation,
Updates & Patches" page, cf.

 http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/download-install

It took a while to realize why you needed Ghostscript, but this is
probably because the internal findPngDevice() tries different PNG
generating functions to find one supported on your system.  One is the
R.utils::png2() device, which calls grDevices::bitmap() which in turn
uses ghostscript.  It is supposed to skip png2() quietly if not
available/working, but I might have the check this again [now on the
very long todo list].

>
> Finally in the QC documentation the command:
>
> plotImage(cf, transform=log2, palette=rainbow(256))
>
> does not work. However, changing it to the following seemed to solve
> the problem:
>
> plotImage(cf, transform=list(log2), palette=rainbow(256))

Thanks for point this out.  This is actually a bug, which will be
fixed in the next release.  In the meanwhile, I've updated the example
online.

Cheers

/Henrik

That's strange.  Make sure you a really in the correct directory, then
try to re-process() the allelic crosstalk again.  If you don't get the
error again, you must have hit a strange glitch (or you run things in
parallel).

It is not clear to me if you are now processing a different data set
or not (the first message did not reveal anything about the script or
dataset names).  If you already did ACC on the dataset, this error
complaining about a tmp file should not occur, because
aroma.affymetrix should definitely detect that the data set was
already processed.  Note, you have to be really careful if you add new
CEL files to already processed data set, i.e. you can get it to work
if you know how it works, but otherwise it is doomed to fail
somewhere.

In either case, now let's solve your most recent problem and when that
works the problem on FLN.

messages.subject: aroma.affymetrix v0.9.5 released
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

aroma.affymetrix v0.9.5 is now available.  Please update with:

source("http://www.braju.com/R/hbLite.R");
hbInstall("aroma.affymetrix");

The most important update in this release is a major step towards
supporting sequence annotation data and modeling of such.  As a
teaser, you will soon be able to do 25-mer nucleotide-position
normalization on any chip type.  Otherwise, it contains a few minor
bug fixes, better exception handling and a bit of internal clean up.
The complete update history is below.

Enjoy!

Henrik

o Added nbrOfCellsPerUnitGroup() and nbrOfCellsPerUnit() for
  AffymetrixCdfFile.
o Renamed getFitFunction() for all PLMs to getFitUnitGroupFunction(),

  are unknown.  Previously such units were not normalized - for

  readDataUnitFragmentLength() of AffymetrixNetAffxCsvFile.

Hi,

On Mon, Oct 20, 2008 at 3:51 PM, yupu <yupu...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi,
>
> I am using aroma.affymetrix to do copy number estimation on
> affymetrix's SNP6.0 data.
>
> I followed the instructions from
> http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/total-copy-number-analysis-6-0
>
> Things went smoothly, untill I realized there is no data point for at
> position 51598 on Chr1 that is corresponding to probe id CN_473963.
>
>>units <- getUnitsOnChromosome(gi,chromosome=1)
>>pos<- getPositions(gi,units=units)
>>bool <- pos == 51598
>> pos[bool]
> integer(0)
>
>
>
> Did I do anything wrong? Or aroma is now dealing with these probes yet
> for the moment?

Don't rely on exact genomic position in order to identify/refer to a
CN variant/probe, because this information tend to get updated
whenever the human genome annotation data is updated.  Doing that is
also error prone to differences in how positions are defined, e.g. if
the first position of a chromsome is 0 or 1 (which might be issue in
this case).

Instead, use the unit name to identify the position and not the other
way around, e.g.

> cdf <- AffymetrixCdfFile$byChipType("GenomeWideSNP_6", tags="Full");
> gi <- getGenomeInformation(cdf);
> unit <- indexOf(cdf, name="CN_473963");
> unit
[1] 935591
> pos <- getPositions(gi, units=unit);
> pos
[1] 51599

If you really want to identify a unit name given a position, allow for
some shift, say +/-5 nucleotides, e.g.

> units <- getUnitsOnChromosome(gi, chromosome=1);
> pos <- getPositions(gi, units=units);
> idxs <- which(51598-5 <= pos & pos <= 51598+5);
> units[idxs];
[1] 935591
> pos[idxs];
[1] 51599

Cheers

/Henrik

>
> Thanks,
> Yupu
> >
>

Is there a vignette for analyzing data from the Gene ST arrays? I am processing some HuGene10st arrays. This is what I came up with so far, but am stuck with regard to how to write the normalized data set as a table or to create an R object:

#Convert CDF downloaded from Affy from ASCII to Binary format
library(affxparser)
convertCdf("HuGene-1_0-st-v1.r3.ASCII.cdf", "HuGene-1_0-st-v1.r3.cdf", verbose=T)

#Copy the binary CDF file to the annotationData directory:

#C:\Program Files (x86)\R\R-2.7.1\library\aroma.affymetrix\annotationData\chipTypes\hugene10stv1
library(aroma.affymetrix)
cdfDirectory <- "C:/Program Files (x86)/R/R-2.7.1/library/aroma.affymetrix/annotationData"

setwd(cdfDirectory)
cdf <- AffymetrixCdfFile$fromChipType("HuGene-1_0-st-v1",tags="r3")

#Download the annotation file and rename to "HuGene-1_0-st-v1_annot.csv" in the appropriate chipTypes directory

csv <- AffymetrixNetAffxCsvFile$byChipType("HuGene-1_0-st-v1", tags="")

#create a rawData/"StudyName"/"ArrayName" directory and copy the cel files to this directory
#e.g. W:\Human_Gene_ST_Test\rawData\MAQC\HuGene-1_0-st-v1
setwd(W:\\Human_Gene_ST_Test\)
dataSet <- "MAQC"
cs <- AffymetrixCelSet$byName(dataSet, cdf=cdf)

#Calibration And Normalization Of Probe Level Data

csBC <- process(bc,verbose=TRUE)
qn <- QuantileNormalization(csBC, typesToUpdate="pm")
csN <- process(qn, verbose=verbose)

#Summarization - IS THIS JUST FOR EXON ARRAYS?
plmTr <- ExonRmaPlm(csN, mergeGroups=TRUE)
fit(plmTr, verbose=verbose) #WHAT DOES THIS STEP DO?

What next? How do you create a text file or an R object for the background corrected, normalized and summarized data? How do you link this to the annotation csv file?

Thanks,

Peter

messages.body_plain:
Hi.

On Tue, Oct 21, 2008 at 8:48 AM, yupu <yupu...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Henrik:
>
> Hi, thanks for the response!
>
> Is there any way for me to find out all available APIs ( or functions)
> that come with the package?
>
> I tried ?getUnitsOnChromosome but there is not much information
> there :-S

I don't have the time to write detailed Rd help pages for end users
(and keep them up to date, which is the time-consuming part).   I do
not know how many functions and methods there are, but we're talking
about more than 1000 pages of code.  However, you can trust that the
usage/synopsis and the arguments are correct for Rd files.  The Rd
help for a lot of the methods/functions are directed to a common page
(explaining it is still to be documented).  The ones that exists are
mostly intended for developers, but developers tend to look at/follow
the source code instead.

Instead, my strategy is to document the package online.  Some features
are also revealed in replies on the mailing list itself - so it's
worth skimming through message from others too.  When a feature
discussed in the forum becomes frequently used, I try to write up a
page or add it to a vignette.
What is there you can trust.  I am very conservative about what parts
of the API I make "public" this way, because for each new
method/feature I expose I will also have to keep backward compatible
which takes time.

The design of classes in aroma.affymetrix can be though of as classic
object-oriented programming as seem in C++, Java etc.  This means that
you have an object of a certain class and there exist methods coupled
to that class.  If you know the class, you can quickly get a list of
methods available, e.g.

messages.subject: Re: [aroma.affymetrix] How do you analyze Gene ST Data?
messages.subject_clean: [aroma.affymetrix] How do you analyze Gene ST Data?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Peter,

I *strongly* (as strong as possible) recommend you to read up on what
the directory structures should look like in order for
aroma.affymetrix to work.  It is essential for all your future work
with aroma.affymetrix.  Start reading here:

 http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/users-guide

There you'll also find out about some very important concepts defined,
e.g. filename, fullname, name, tags.  If you understand that, you will
see how it works and how to name your directories and where to put
what.

I think it would also help you understand how the package works, if
you worked through (not just reading) some of the other vignettes.
That should be easier to troubleshoot and then you'll see what new
directories and files are created as you go.

A general comment, which is useful for everyone:

If you find yourself specifying paths or full pathname in your main
aroma.affymetrix scripts, you are doing something wrong.  The package
is design to work without having to specify paths.  A rule of thumb is
that you should be able to move any aroma.affymetrix script to another
computer system and run it without having to change anything.

I will try to give more comments below, but not to detailed as I think
you will better know what's going on yourself after doing the above.
You'll see that it is not that hard (I hope it is even intuitive and
consistent when you know the pattern).

On Tue, Oct 21, 2008 at 6:33 AM,  <pwhi...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Is there a vignette for analyzing data from the Gene ST arrays? I am
> processing some HuGene10st arrays.

No, there is no such vignette currently.  Maybe your efforts could end
up creating such?

> This is what I came up with so far, but
> am stuck with regard to how to write the normalized data set as a table or
> to create an R object:
>
> #Convert CDF downloaded from Affy from ASCII to Binary format
> library(affxparser)
> convertCdf("HuGene-1_0-st-v1.r3.ASCII.cdf", "HuGene-1_0-st-v1.r3.cdf",
> verbose=T)

Yes, you should always work with binary CDFs (way faster and more
efficient).  You should also rename the binary CDF slightly different
by replacing ".r3" with ",r3".  This is important and you understand
why when you understand the concepts of filename, fullname, name and
tags.  Then you will be able to "load" the CDF as illustrated in:

http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/hugene-1-0-st

>
> #Copy the binary CDF file to the annotationData directory:
> #C:\Program Files
> (x86)\R\R-2.7.1\library\aroma.affymetrix\annotationData\chipTypes\hugene10stv1

Reading the above, you will for instance find out that the
'hugene10stv1' is not correct, because it does not match the
'chiptype' of the CDF.

> library(aroma.affymetrix)
> cdfDirectory <- "C:/Program Files
> (x86)/R/R-2.7.1/library/aroma.affymetrix/annotationData"
> setwd(cdfDirectory)

So, you should never have to do this (see above).

> cdf <- AffymetrixCdfFile$fromChipType("HuGene-1_0-st-v1",tags="r3")

I guess you get an error here, because you named the binary CDF
incorrectly (see above).

>
> #Download the annotation file and rename to "HuGene-1_0-st-v1_annot.csv" in
> the appropriate chipTypes directory
> csv <- AffymetrixNetAffxCsvFile$byChipType("HuGene-1_0-st-v1", tags="")

In the below code, there is nothing in this NetAffx CSV that is
needed/used.  So, at this stage, I wouldn't worry about that file.

>
> #create a rawData/"StudyName"/"ArrayName" directory and copy the cel files
> to this directory
> #e.g. W:\Human_Gene_ST_Test\rawData\MAQC\HuGene-1_0-st-v1
> setwd(W:\\Human_Gene_ST_Test\)
> dataSet <- "MAQC"

Ditto.

> cs <- AffymetrixCelSet$byName(dataSet, cdf=cdf)
>
> #Calibration And Normalization Of Probe Level Data
> bc <- RmaBackgroundCorrection(cs, tag="MAQC")

You should have to add tags here - maybe later that'll make sense, but
for your initial purposes just skip it.  Details: You are actually
overriding the tags here, not adding, cf. tags="MAQS" and
tags="*,MAQS".

> csBC <- process(bc,verbose=TRUE)
> qn <- QuantileNormalization(csBC, typesToUpdate="pm")
> csN <- process(qn, verbose=verbose)
>
> #Summarization - IS THIS JUST FOR EXON ARRAYS?
> plmTr <- ExonRmaPlm(csN, mergeGroups=TRUE)
> fit(plmTr, verbose=verbose) #WHAT DOES THIS STEP DO?

Please read the other vignettes etc, but yes, ExonRmaPlm is designed
specifically from exon arrays.

>
> What next? How do you create a text file or an R object for the background
> corrected, normalized and summarized data?

This has been discussed frequently on the mailing list and some of the
vignettes illustrate this too.  There are methods such as
extractMatrix(), extractDataFrame(), and extractTheta() that will be
useful to you.  The latter is only documented in my replies on the
mailing list (See archive/Discussion section).

> How do you link this to the
> annotation csv file?

You'll have to explain what you mean by "link".

Hope this help you get started

Henrik

>
> Thanks,
>
> Peter
>
>
>
> >
>

messages.body_plain:
Just to add a couple notes to Henrik's reply.  After you've got all
the directories sorted out, you can:

1. Process Gene 1.0 ST data much the same as Exon array data, except
that you'll need to replace 'ExonRmaPlm' with 'RmaPlm' (and you won't
be able to run FIRMA).  See:
http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/human-exon-array-analysis

2. To save one step, you should be able to just download the binary
CDF from the link at the bottom of:
http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/hugene-1-0-st
(I've made binary CDFs of the Rat and Mouse Gene 1.0 ST chips as well)

3. After a series of steps (RMA bg adjustment, quantile normalization,
probe level modelling), as Henrik mentioned you can use
extractDataFrame to get a table of summarized expression values for
every probeset.

Hope that helps.

Cheers,
Mark

location of the TSS for each unit.

extra terms in the model, or at least having an R version of it.

messages.body_plain:
Hi.

On Wed, Oct 22, 2008 at 2:19 PM, pwhiteusa <pwhi...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Dear Henrik and Mark,
>
> Thanks so much for your replies. I am going to work through your
> responses and try again. I did get confused by the directory structure
> and naming conventions. What I would like to do is have all of my
> annotation files in one location (Network Drive W) as these are shared
> by multiple folks in my group. The we I perform an experiment I would
> like all analysis and output that is generated to be stored in the
> appropriate directory on a different location (Network Drive X). As I
> understand the aroma.affymetrix directory requirements, everything
> must be in the rawData and the annotationData directories, both of
> which must be in the same path. Is that correct?

Yes, it is correct that aroma.affymetrix needs to see annotationData/
and rawData/ in the current working directory.   This is on purpose
and design to make life easier (indeed).  This way we do not have to
specify paths in our scripts, because aroma.affymetrix knows where to
look for them.  Also, all users will have the same setup, there are
less degrees of freedom for mistakes, and fluent users can quickly
pick out what mistakes beginners does, and all scripts work the same
everywhere.

So, how to work with this setup  in practice?  On Unix-like systems
this is easy because you can just create so called soft links pointing
such directories to other places on the file system.  From R and
aroma.affymetrix, they look the same as regular directories.  This way
multiple people can share the same data directories.  Unfortunately,
there is no such feature on MS Windows file system.  However, I added
support for/follow Windows Shortcut Links, which allow us to emulate
this.  Thus, you can create a shortcut in the current directory that
points to the real directory.  You can verify that it works by
double-clicking on the link in the Windows Explorer and the
orginal/real directory should open.  I use it all the time on my
Windows notebook.   This also allows me to keep one working directory
per project.

In your case, say your working directory is,
C:/Users/pwhiteusa/projectA/, then you want to create the following
Windows Shortcut links:

  C:/Users/pwhiteusa/projectA/annotationData[.lnk] -> W:/annotationData/
  C:/Users/pwhiteusa/projectA/rawData[.lnk] -> W:/rawData/

Similarly, you can pre-create output directories to go elsewhere, e.g.

  C:/Users/pwhiteusa/projectA/probeData[.lnk] -> X:/probeData/
  C:/Users/pwhiteusa/projectA/plmData[.lnk] -> X:/plmData/
  C:/Users/pwhiteusa/projectA/cbsData[.lnk] -> X:/cbsData/
  C:/Users/pwhiteusa/projectA/firmaData[.lnk] -> X:/firmaData/

Note that you have to create those directories under X:/.

I write [.lnk], because depending on your setup the filename extension
*.lnk will be visible or not.  On a default Windows setup they are
typically not, so then then shortcuts will look like regular
directories/files.

Also, you can create shortcuts for subdirectories too.  For instance,
you may have a setup like this:

  C:/Users/pwhiteusa/projectA/annotationData/chipTypes/  # A real directory
  C:/Users/pwhiteusa/projectA/annotationData/chipTypes/Mapping50K_Hind240/
# A real directory
  C:/Users/pwhiteusa/projectA/annotationData/chipTypes/GenomeWideSNP_6[.lnk]
 # A link to
                         ->
W:/annotationData/chipTypes/GenomeWideSNP_6/  # ...a directory
elsewhere

This allows different people to maintain different chip types etc.

For troubleshooting Windows Shortcuts, this might help:

library("R.utils");
path <- Arguments$getReadablePath("annotationData");
print(path);

If your annotationData[.lnk] in the current directory points to an
existing directory, you should see that directory, e.g.
W:/annotationData/.

Hope this helps

Henrik

>
> Thanks,
>
> Peter

messages.subject: Re: Updating affxparser on Linux server
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

you the way the BioC installation scripts are setup, is that it will
require everyone to use the most recent version of R and since R
v2.8.0 was release last week, R v2.7.x is outdated in their
perspective.  Hence you will not get access to the BioC v2.3
repository (just release) but only the previous version BioC v2.2
(last half year).   If you happen to run the new developers/alpha/beta
version of R, R v2.9.0dev, you will get access to BioC v2.4 repository
where all developers/alpha/beta version of the BioC packages sits.
This is described (somewhere) on the BioC webpage and make sure you
understand it if you're going to use a lot BioC packages.

So, with R v2.7.0 you only get access to BioC v2.2 but the required
version affxparser is in BioC v2.3.   You should update R to R v2.8.0
- that'll help you.  However, in the meanwhile, I've provided a "hack"
that allows you to install packages from BioC v2.3 although you run R
v2.7.x:

source("http://www.bioconductor.org/biocLite.R")
biocLite("affxparser", rver="2.8.0")

This will trick the BioC installation scripts to think you're running
R v2.8.0.

Then you should get affxparser v1.14.0 (I think).

/Henrik

This is great and I think it is possible too - we might have to
fine/adjust aroma.affymetrix slightly, but lets see.

>
> One question.  You have UGP (UnitGroupPosition) files - AromaUgpFile
> objects.  For you, each unit is (usually) a SNP and therefore would
> have one genomic location.  For me, each unit is a promoter and then
> each probe within a promoter has its own position, typically non-
> regular spacing as well.  I'll probably also need to store strand and
> location of the TSS for each unit.

You probably meant to write this, but the UGP is actually for Unit
*Genome* Position and maps (unit, chromosome, position), where the
'unit' [index] is implicit by the order.  For other who are
interested, more info at:

  http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/unit-genome-position-ugp-files

Yes, the UGP annotation data is unit centric and units are defined by
the CDF.  The class that handles UGP maps/files is the AromaUgpFile
class.   For more general unit-based mappings, i.e. (unit, <data>,
<data2>, ...), there is the AromaUnitTabularBinaryFile.  The
AromaUgpFile is actually a special case of this class.  For info of
the former, see also:

http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/creating-aromaunittabularfile-from-scratch

In turn the superclass of AromaUnitTabularBinaryFile is
AromaUnitTabularBinaryFile, cf:

http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/aromatabularbinaryfile

Think of it as a binary tab delimited file where each column holds a
predefined data type of certain size (string are not supported).

Another natural way of indexing annotation data according to the CDF
is by not only units but also groups, e.g. here (unit, group,
chromosome, position).  There is no class available for this mapping.

Leaving the constraints of the CDF we can also index by probes/cells,
e.g. here (cell, chromosome, position).  Such annotation data is
independent of the CDF and if you change the CDF you can still use the
same map because there is a mapping from the CDF to the cells.  As you
found out, there is indeed a class for this, namely
AromaCellTabularBinaryFile.  Analogously to how
AromaUnitTabularBinaryFile index data by units, this new class index
data by cell indices.  Likewise, you can define you own set of columns
(data type and size).  For (cell, chromosome, position), you need to
create a AromaCgpFile class which replicated AromaUgpFile but for
cells.  You already learned about the AromaCellSequenceFile, and if
you look at the code it is actually inheriting from
AromaCellTabularBinaryFile, because the latter has some general
methods that can be useful.

> Is there an easy way to store this info in the AromaUgpFiles?  Or, a
> simple extension of it?

So, you need to create a AromaCgpFile class for this.

Yes, it stores the sequences in raw columns, such that the 1st
nucleotide of each probe sequence is in the 1st column, the 2nd
nucleotide in the 2nd column and so on until the 25th probe position.
The nucleotide is encoded as a raw/single byte.  Storing it column by
column makes it faster to grab for instance the middle base of all
probes, or say the middle 3 bases.  The 26th column hold information
on target strand.   AromaCellSequenceFile inherit from
AromaCellTabularBinaryFile, so we can reuse a lot.

>
> AromaCellTabularBinaryFile will allow me to store one other thing for
> every cell (e.g. match scores -- the number of hits to the genome, etc).

Yes.

>
> The genomic positions is the tricky bit, because some probes map to
> multiple locations.  As you mentioned previously, I could associate
> multiple TabularBinaryFiles and for the probes (cells) that map to
> multiple locations populate it.

I recall our chat about this.

CASE 1: SMALL UPPER BOUND OF NUMBER OF POSITIONS PER CELL
If there there is no probe with more than K mappings and K is small,
then I would just allocate the 2*K columns needed and store NAs where
there are no mappings.  Example map:

 (cell, chromosome[1], position[1], ..., , chromosome[K], position[K])

CASE 2: SMALL UPPER BOUND OF NUMBER OF POSITIONS PER CELL
In case K is too large, I would find the most common number of
mappings, say K*, and use CASE 1 to store the K* first mappings.  You
might want to add a column specifying the nbrOfLoci for each cell:

 (cell, nbrOfLoci, chromosome[1], position[1], ..., , chromosome[K*],
position[K*])

and then deal with the exceptions separately.  This way you will have
quickly access/indexing in most of the cases, i.e. when nbrOfLoci <=
K*.  For the cells where nbrOfLoci > K*, you need to figure out how to
store that data in the same file.  It is possible, but it is not clear
how to do it.  In one way or the other, you need to allocate space
(think memory) for this extra data and you need to be able to find it.
 Basically, you need to encode some kind of ragged list structure.
You can allocate extra space by adding auxiliary columns.  You have to
create your own mapping and encoding for what you want though.  Then
your API is the one that will hide all the details.  Another
alternatives is to store the extra mappings in new rows, but you have
to come up with a way to index these rows.  Same problem to solve.
(Avoid using the file footer to store this kind of data).

The performance will depend on how ragged or how rectangular your map is.

You'll also have to think how you should return data. You might want
to return data as a list structure, where each element correspond to a
cell and holds a vector of positions.

To make sure I understand you correct: In your CDF, the same cell
index can show up in multiple units, correct?

The closest to this idea is how we read data from CEL files in the
shape of the CDF.  This is done by the affxparser package.  However,
if the same cell index occur in several units, all you'll get is the
same probe intensity read in all places.  It is not possible to read
different values.

So, there is no such CDF-like structure in aroma.affymetrix, except
the CDF/AffymetrixCdfFile itself.  You could of course create a CDF
file that holds the data you wish to store (you can even encode other
data types in the existing CDF ones as long as it fits).  The you
could create a subclass to AffymetrixCdfFile that hides all the
details.

Before deciding on a file format, maybe it is easier to just "dump"
(using saveObject()) a precreated list structure like the one you show
above and then setup up a class that hides all the details.
Internally it can use loadObject() to read the structure back ones.
Special readUnits() functions will then emulate the access similar to
how it is done for CDFs.  This will allow you to procrastinate your
decision on the file format you need to use.

I was suggesting that you keep you current CDF as is, and have another
that carries the genomic locations.  For instance, you can encode the
'chromosome' location in 'pbase', and 'position' in 'atom'.  If 'atom'
only holds a short (2 bytes), you'll need to encode it in 'indexpos'
as well.  This file will formally not be a CDF but you can probably
use the Fusion SDK to read it.  I would also have a different file
name ending for it.   It is also important that it is clear to what
CDF this "parallel CDF" maps to.

My feeling is that it is better to avoid using the CDF file format for
this, because it is likely to cause problems one day or the other for
either you or the end user.  I can see how the wrong "parallel CDF" is
used for a different CDF and so on.  Your encoding (pbase, atom &
indexpos) -> (chromosome, position) has to be done each time you read
and probably at the R level, which means that it will be rather slow
(this type of encoding is done when we save PLM fits, and we know it
takes time).

A mapping independent of your CDF is:

(cell, chromsome1, position1, chromsome2, position2, ..., chromsomeK,
positionK) (**)

where K varies with cell.  This is basically a ragged list.  To speed
things up you can collect you cells into block of equal K size, such
that each block becomes a rectangular matrix.  In your case you will
have blocks of 10 different sizes.   Each block can be an element in a
list.  To access the above mapping (**) given a cell index, you will
have to have a mapping/hash that first brings you to the right block,
and then to the right row of that block.

Yet again, I think it will be useful to first do this in R without
worrying about the file format; use save-/loadObject() to hide that
from the user.

}

thanks
Manisha

messages.subject: Re: merging the NSP & STY chip data for the 500
messages.subject_clean: merging the NSP & STY chip data for the 500
messages.body_plain:
Hi there,

I read your post, by a complete random sequence of events. The problem
that you are asking emerged at our department as well. I have created
a standalone program that combines the fragments/CNVs from both the
Affymetrix NSP and STY chips. The input for the program comes from the
Affymetrix genotyping console (downloadable from affy’s website).
If you are still interested in this problem you could contact me on my
e-mail and I could send you the program.
The program uses the sample ID (contains chip position- i.e. NPS or
STY), Gain or Loss, N markers, Start linear position, End linear
position and Chromosome. All these parameters are coming from the
Genotyping console, but this text file could be created from any
program. You could also specify a number of parameters in my program:
KB overlap between the two chips for each sample ID, maximum position
if no overlap (use it or not), minimum position if overlap (use it or
not), Start position (minimum or maximum), End position (minimum or
maximum) and you could export the result into a file.

If you are interested you could contact me, via e-mail:
Ivan...@cf.ac.uk

Regards,
Dobril Ivanov
Cardiff University/ Biostatistics and Bioinformatics Unit

messages.subject_clean: [aroma.affymetrix] Require more SNP6.0 array sample or not ?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

On Sat, Oct 25, 2008 at 4:19 AM, nongnone <anunc...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Dear All,
> I am working on CNV mapping with SNP6.0. I have no idea to analyze
> them because I have only two samples (male and female). I would like
> to ask you for more information. Are two chips analyzed in your
> algorithm effect the CNV results ? I mean that the small sample size
> of chip effect the normalization or whatever step in your algorithm ?

My first question is what is your biological question/hypothesis
making you analyze only two single samples?  That is a key question
for your analysis.  What you expect to learn from CN estimates of two
samples alone?  Are you doing personalized diagnostics?

I'm not sure which "algorithm" you refer to, but I guess you are
referring to the CRMA method.  If so, please read:

H. Bengtsson; R. Irizarry; B. Carvalho; T. Speed, Estimation and
assessment of raw copy numbers at the single locus level,
Bioinformatics, 2008. [pmid: 18204055] [doi:
10.1093/bioinformatics/btn016]

carefully.  There are also references to the other related methods
used in that study and those will give you more insights in CN
analysis.

Any microarray-based CN analysis requires some kind of reference to
which the sample of interest is compared to.  This is pretty much the
case for all microarray analysis, not just CN ones.  Your problem is
to choose/find a reference.

If you use the "default" CRMA processing steps, you are probably using
the pool of all arrays as a proxy for your reference.  In your case
this means that you take the average of only two arrays, which is not
a good idea.  This is basically the same as doing a pairwise CN
analysis of the two samples, which I guess you don't want.

As I've suggested others on this list (search archive) a few times: If
you have too few arrays in your data set, then try to get more
anonymous/dummy arrays from the *same* microarray facility, because
they will add to your pool to calculate the average reference, and
in-house data is always less noisy than external data.  Some people
suggest to use publicly available HapMap CEL files (you have to order
them; free), but I and others have found that this adds much more
variability to the estimates.

Cheers

/Henrik

> Pls provide more information about that. Thank you for advanced. I am
> looking forward your help (information).
>
> Thank you so much
> Anunchai Assawamkin
>
> >
>

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

the mistake you are doing is that you tell R/aroma.affymetrix to
process both chip types, but you only have/load data for one of them.
You do:

chipTypes <- c("Mapping50K_Hind240", "Mapping50K_Xba240")

and this is what is used in the for loops.  If you only want to
process one of the chip types, the simplest modification you can do to
solve the problem is to replace the above with:

chipTypes <- "Mapping50K_Hind240"

I recommend that you read up a bit more on R - it'll help
troubleshoot/detect these problems.  In the meanwhile, I've updated
the Vignette 'Paired total copy number analysis' to be robust against
this kind of mistakes.

Cheers

Henrik

messages.subject: Interpretation of QC Spacial Images
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I'm using aroma.affymetrix to plot QC spatial images (PlotImage) and was wondering if there is any documentation that would help further interpret the images.  As per the documentation, the plots are super helpful in determining standout regions that are banded or bubble-ish.  I'm plotting the Log2 transform mapped onto a rainbow palette.  Is it true that light colors map to regions of low intensity and vice versa?

Any insights you may have with regard to gleaning information from the images would be helpful.

Thanks in advance.
Andy

messages.subject: Re: [aroma.affymetrix] Interpretation of QC Spacial Images
messages.body_plain:
Hi.

On Tue, Oct 28, 2008 at 9:30 AM, Andy Reynolds <arey...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi,
> I'm using aroma.affymetrix to plot QC spatial images (PlotImage) and was
> wondering if there is any documentation that would help further interpret
> the images.  As per the documentation, the plots are super helpful in
> determining standout regions that are banded or bubble-ish.  I'm plotting
> the Log2 transform mapped onto a rainbow palette.  Is it true that light
> colors map to regions of low intensity and vice versa?

I guess you are referring to 'rainbow' in setup like this:

ae <- ArrayExplorer(rsList);
setColorMaps(ae, c("log2,log2neg,rainbow", "log2,log2pos,rainbow"));
process(ae, verbose=log);

That 'rainbow' string is actually referring to the name of an existing
functions, i.e. here rainbow().  You can set the range and order of
colors generated by such a function by doing something like:

col <- rainbow(256);
plot(seq(along=col), col=col, pch=19, cex=2);

As you see, the intensity/brightness of the rainbow() palette is *not*
linear.  There are other palettes you can try, e.g. terrain.colors()
etc.  See the help pages for one of them and you'll find more.  The
r-help list is a good list to ask for more info on this.

BTW, in the above ArrayExplorer example (see also last figure in
http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/generic-quality-assessment),
the "white" (transparent actually) dots (can also) indicate missing
values.

Hope this helps

Henrik

>
> Any insights you may have with regard to gleaning information from the
> images would be helpful.
>
> Thanks in advance.
> Andy
>
> >

messages.subject: Re: [aroma.affymetrix] QuantileNormalization
messages.body_plain:
Hi.

On Tue, Oct 28, 2008 at 2:25 PM, Venkat <vese...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi:
>
> Is it possible to provide a specific list of probe names (from the SNP
> chip) for the subsetToAvg argument in the QuantileNormalization
> function in order to normalize based only a pre-defined subset?

Yes, because the 'subsetToAvg' argument takes a vector of cell indices
(alt. a scalar in (0,1] to indicate a deterministic fraction of all
cell indices).  So, you need to find the cell indices for the units
(==SNPs/CN loci) of interest.  If you know the unit indices you can
use getCellIndices(cdf, ...) to get the cell indices.  To find the
unit indices based on unit names, you can use indexOf(cdf, ...).
Example:

> cdf <- AffymetrixCdfFile$byChipType("GenomeWideSNP_6", tags="Full");
> unitNames <- c("SNP_A-4214079", "SNP_A-2001454", "CN_453850")
> units <- indexOf(cdf, names=unitNames);
> str(units);
 int [1:3] 1001 1002 980123
> cells <- getCellIndices(cdf, units=units, unlist=TRUE, useNames=FALSE);
> cells <- sort(cells);
> str(cells);
 int [1:13] 133501 133502 588881 588882 640619 640620 3418844 4756905 4756
05565 ...

>
> Also there is a QuantileNormalization step in the vignette for the
> total copy number analysis for the 500k chips but not GWS6 chips.  Is
> the QuantileNormalization step available and correct for GWS6 chips?

The QuantileNormalization class/method works for any Affymetrix chip type.

There are many different ways to pre-process data out there and the
two vignettes show to different ways.

I should really put up a CRMA (v1) vignette illustrating the exact
steps in the Bengtsson et al. (2008) paper or CRMA preprocessing (our
preferred method) of 500K (and before), but short of time...  Although
developed for 500K (before GWS5/6 came out), the CRMA model (with some
modifications) actually applies to GWS5/GWS6 arrays too.  If replacing
AvgCnPlm with RlmCnPlm in the GWS6 vignette, you actually have CRMA.
Of course, there are some hidden details taking care of the
multi-enzyme hybridization etc, but the main idea is the same.  There
will soon also be a CRMA v2 method that we developed for GWS5/6 (but
will be backward compatible with all generations of SNP/CN chip
types).  The major news will be that it also does sequence-based
normalization and is a single-array preprocessing method.  Stay
tuned... (there will for sure be a CRMA v2 vignette).

Cheers

Henrik

>
> Thanks,
> Venkat
>
> >
>

than the default CN=2.  I'll have to look into this, e.g. create a
redundancy test, check the code etc.  That will take some time.

> BTW: the reports file produced has a tag "Paired", is this expected?

Yes, that is because when you pass 'ceRef' as the references then the
CbsModel thinks it is a paired setup (which is the most common case).
There is currently no public API for changing this, but you can do
[use with care as it may change] by:

> print(getTags(cbs, collapse=","))
[1] "ACC,-XY,RMA,+300,A+B,FLN,-XY,paired"
> cbs$.paired <- FALSE   # <==
> print(getTags(cbs, collapse=","))

On Tue, Oct 28, 2008 at 3:52 PM, Venkat <vese...@gmail.com> wrote:

>> two vignettes show to different ways.
>>
>> I should really put up a CRMA (v1) vignette illustrating the exact
>> steps in the Bengtsson et al. (2008) paper or CRMA preprocessing (our
>> preferred method) of 500K (and before), but short of time...  Although
>> developed for 500K (before GWS5/6 came out), the CRMA model (with some
>> modifications) actually applies to GWS5/GWS6 arrays too.  If replacing
>> AvgCnPlm with RlmCnPlm in the GWS6 vignette, you actually have CRMA.
>
> As a followup is it redundant to do
>
>  qn <- QuantileNormalization(csC)
>  csN <- process(qn, verbose=verbose)
>
> prior to
>
>  plm <- RmaCnPlm(csN, mergeStrands=TRUE, combineAlleles=FALSE, shift=
> +300)
>  fit(plm, verbose=verbose)
>
> i.e. will the plm fit from RmaCnPlm with and without the
> QuantileNormalization step be the same.

No.

I see your confusion: The "Rma" part of "RmaCnPlm" is referring to the
RMA-style probe summarization (=the log-additive model) and not any of
the other parts of the RMA model.  Thus, it does not include QN.  We
chosed to call it Rma*Plm to show the origin of the probe-level model
(PLM).  LogAdditivePlm was discussed but we though it was not specific
enough.  We also have dChip's Mbei*Plm, and ours Affine*Plm (also a
multiplicative model related to MBEI) and Avg*Plm.

>
> And if so does  RmaCnPlm  have a  subsetToAvg  argument.

So, no, because it fit the log-additive model to each unit separately
(across arrays).

Hope this clarifies a few things

Henrik

> Venkat

On Wed, Oct 29, 2008 at 2:39 AM, armand.v...@gmail.com
<armand....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Dear all,

>> AffymetrixCelSet$fromName(name="10thserie,ACC,ra,-XY,AVG,+300,A+B,FLN,-XY",cdf=cdf,paths="plmData")
> forcing the path to plmData, and using the same cdf than used during
> the analysis.

What I still recommend is to just rerun the complete script from
start.  The package will detect which steps are already processed and
skip them.  The overhead for doing this that it takes a little while
for aroma.affymetrix to verify that a step is actually complete,
before moving to the next.  I use this more or less all the time.

At the end, I'll show how to do what you are trying to do:

>
> However, I catch an exception complaining that the current cdf is
> different from the one used during the analysis. It seems the number
> of cells do not match.

Yes, this is because the CEL set you are trying to "load" consists of
so called chip-effect CEL files, which has less cells ("probes") and
these cells are mapped according to a so called monocell CDF. There is
a bit on monocell CDFs on Page 'Setting up annotation files':

  http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/setup

In your case you are trying to use the original CDF, but you really
need the monocell CDF, e.g.

> cdf <- AffymetrixCdfFile$byChipType("GenomeWideSNP_5", tags="Full,r2");
> cdf
AffymetrixCdfFile:

Path: C:/Users/hb/Documents/My Data/annotationData/chipTypes/GenomeWideSNP_5

> cdfM <- getMonocellCdf(cdf);
> cdfM
AffymetrixCdfFile:
Path: C:/Users/hb/Documents/My Data/annotationData/chipTypes/GenomeWideSNP_5
Filename: GenomeWideSNP_5,Full,r2,monocell.CDF
Filesize: 208.28MB
Chip type: GenomeWideSNP_5,Full,r2,monocell

RAM: 0.00MB
File format: v4 (binary; XDA)

Dimension: 1201x1201
Number of cells: 1442401
Number of units: 920928
Cells per unit: 1.57

Number of QC units: 6

That explains the error message.

> Have you experienced such problem before ? Or am I just doing
> something wrong ?

Next: "If you find yourself specifying paths or full pathname in your main
aroma.affymetrix scripts, you are doing something wrong.  The package
is design to work without having to specify paths.  A rule of thumb is
that you should be able to move any aroma.affymetrix script to another
computer system and run it without having to change anything." [thread
'How do you analyze Gene ST Data?', Oct 21, 2008].

To "load" an existing chip-effect set, do:

cdf <- AffymetrixCdfFile$byChipType("GenomeWideSNP_5", tags="Full,r2");
cdfM <- getMonocellCdf(cdf);
dataSet <- "10thserie";
tags <- "ACC,ra,-XY,AVG,+300,A+B,FLN,-XY";
cesN <- CnChipEffectSet$byName(dataSet, tags=tags, cdf=cdfM,
mergeStrands=TRUE, combineAlleles=TRUE);

If you do not explicitly specify the arguments 'mergeStrands' and
'combineAlleles', these has to be inferred from the data itself, which
will take some time.  To avoid this overhead, specify it explicitly.
It is important that you use the same value as when you fitted the
PLM.

Note that you have to specify class 'CnChipEffectSet', because that is
the class of the chip-effect set you are loading.  It is true that
this is a subset of AffymetrixCelSet, but if you use the latter (as
you did), you will get an object that is of that class.

FYI, use byName() instead of deprecated alias fromName().  For my
information (so I can correct it), is there documentation online that
still use fromName()?  Where did you learn about this?

Hope this helps

Henrik

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm using FIRMA in order to detect alternative  splicing. I have read
the paper and I'm trying the algorithm with the same datasets from
Affymetrix (Panel of tissue samples and Colon cancer data) but I don't
get the same results. For example I don't get enrichment in firma
scores for exons of muscle specificity (i.e. 2429323 for UNR) or
enrichment in firma scores in cancer splicing (i.e. 3569830 for
ACTN1).

This is my script in R:

library(aroma.affymetrix)
setwd('/home/arisueno/microarrays/firma')

verbose <- Arguments$getVerbose(-8)
timestampOn(verbose)

name<-"tissues"
chipType<-"HuEx-1_0-st-v2"

cs<-AffymetrixCelSet$fromName(name, chipType=chipType)
print(cs)

bc<-RmaBackgroundCorrection(cs)
csBC<-process(bc,verbose=verbose)
qn<-QuantileNormalization(csBC, typesToUpdate="pm")
print(qn)
csN <- process(qn, verbose=verbose)

print(csN)

plm <- ExonRmaPlm(csN, mergeGroups=TRUE)
print(plm)
fit(plm, verbose=verbose)

firma <- FirmaModel(plm)
fit(firma, verbose=verbose)
fs <-getFirmaScores(firma)

df<-extractDataFrame(fs, units=NULL, addNames = TRUE)
m<-cbind(df[,1],log2(df[,6:38]))

Is this correct?

Thanks in advance.

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

this is probably due to a corrupt transfer of the CEL file.

Since the area under each curve should be one, it is clear that for
the red curve some of the density is not shown.  I'm quite sure it is
all your zeros that are not shown, because they are all -Inf on the
log-scale.  So, you have a lot of zeros in Array #91 (and maybe others
too).  Why?  See below.  How to avoid/detect it?  See below.

I've seen this myself and I know of at least one more case where a CEL
file looked perfectly fine, but it had a lot of zeros.  In my case I
copied the files to an external harddrive, [flew across the world],
and copied them to another server.  It was only by chance from looking
at spatial plots that I discovered perfectly horizontal short white
stripes all over the place - these were all due to zero signals.  When
I looked at the CEL file, not only the intensities, but also the
stddvs and the number of pixels were all zeros, which didn't make
sense.  I went back to the source server and ran MD5
[http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MD5] on each CEL file to generate
hashcodes and discovered that my files there and here didn't match.
Something when wrong in the transfer.  I believe it might have to do
with copying to an external USB drive.  One hypothesis I have is that
first an empty file of the *correct size* on the drive is allocated,
and then the file is copied block by block.  Blocks are transfer via
the computers file cache it might have been that all blocks were not
written to the drive.  This is why you have to "eject" the drive
before pulling the USB cable (I think I did it in my case, but I
cannot remember).

To avoid this, when you transfer CEL files, the safest is to gzip/zip
them, because that will detect if something went wrong.  You cannot
gunzip/unzip a file having patches of missing blocks (zeros).  That
will give an error.

I would go back to the source of where you've got the CEL file and
retransfer it (if it still exists).

If you have aroma.affymetrix installed on your source computer as
well, then you can generate MD5 checksums before transferring the
files, by doing:

cdf <- AffymetrixCdfFile$byChipType("Mapping250K_Sty");
cs <- AffymetrixCelSet$byName("snp_all", cdf=cdf);
res <- lapply(cs, writeChecksum);

which will generated *.CEL.md5 files.  Then copy/transfer both *.CEL
and *.CEL.md5 files.  On the new computer, do:

cdf <- AffymetrixCdfFile$byChipType("Mapping250K_Sty");
cs <- AffymetrixCelSet$byName("snp_all", cdf=cdf);
res <- lapply(cs, validateChecksum);

This will *validate* each CEL file against the known MD5 checksum (the
value in the *.CEL.md5 file).  If a discrepancy is found, an error
will be thrown.

You can use the above approach to generate *.CEL.md5 files on the
source computer, copy only the *.CEL.md5 files to your existing
directory and run the validation test.  That will help you identify
which files when wrong.  Your Array #91 will give an error if the
zeros were introduced during the transfer.

Hope this helps

Henrik

reported in this step that you don't understand, let us know, but
otherwise I leave it to you (or one of your collegues) to troubleshoot
this.

Also, I am starting to assume that you cut'n'paste code into the R
prompt.  That is useful for very small analysis, but for longer you
should certainly write your script in an *.R file and run it using
source().  If you do that, any error will interrupt your script from
continuing.

It is rather important that you understand how basic concepts such as
lists in work in R in order to complete and trust your analysis.
Without that understanding you will not be able to troubleshoot what
is going, and you will get stuck in the most basic steps.  I suggest
that you pick up one of the introductory books/manuals/courses on R.

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

if you look carefully at the following code:

for(chiptype in names(csRawList)) {
  cs <- csRawList[[chipType]]
  [...]
  csAccList[[chipType]]<- csAcc
}

you'll see that the for loop is using iterator variable 'chiptype'
whereas you get and assign the elements in the lists using 'chipType'.
 They are not the same variables.   The value of 'chipType' remains
the same through-out the for loop and therefore is the same name used
twice to assign the csAccList.  It's value is the value set in the
last iteration of the previous for loop (when loading the data sets)
and is 'Mapping50K_Xba240'.

Hope this solves your problem

Henrik

messages.subject: how to extract raw copy numbers for paired analysis of 100K
messages.subject_clean: how to extract raw copy numbers for paired analysis of 100K
messages.body_plain:
Hi Henrik,

I am interested in extracting raw copy numbers for my paired analysis
I did on 100K samples. As I understand it ,the vignette for extracting
raw copy numbers is for "Total copy number". The
extractRawCopyNumbers() extracts one array and one chromosome at a
time.

Is there a way to extract raw copy numbers for all chromosomes and all
arrays together for paired analysis?

thanks
manisha

messages.subject_clean: [aroma.affymetrix] how to extract raw copy numbers for paired analysis of 100K
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

On Thu, Oct 30, 2008 at 8:50 PM, biobee <manis...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Henrik,
>
> I am interested in extracting raw copy numbers for my paired analysis
> I did on 100K samples. As I understand it ,the vignette for extracting
> raw copy numbers is for "Total copy number". The
> extractRawCopyNumbers() extracts one array and one chromosome at a
> time.

Yes, extractRawCopyNumbers() is only for that.  To extract from more
chromosomes it has to be called repeatedly with different values of
argument 'chromosome'.  Same for argument 'array'.

>
> Is there a way to extract raw copy numbers for all chromosomes and all
> arrays together for paired analysis?

You have to calculate them "manually" from the chip effects (theta)
for the test and the reference samples, cf. Vignette 'Calculating raw
total copy numbers manually'.

See also recent thread 'How to extract all CNs?' on Oct 13, 2008
[http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/browse_thread/thread/8efa8b64c506b5a7].

Cheers

Henrik

>

> manisha

Hmm, looks alright to me.

Next troubleshooting is to see if the file is corrupt or can cannot be
read for some reason.

First, try:

path <- "annotationData/chipTypes/GenomeWideSNP_6/";
filename <- "GenomeWideSNP_6,Full,na24,HB20080214.ugp";
ugp <- AromaUgpFile(filename, path=path);
print(ugp);  # Important to try this one
...
print(getFileSize(ugp));
[1] 9407568
print(getChecksum(ugp));  # Verify correctness of file
[1] "7b29405939b1bf2cb018956c4003de02"

If that works, then try:

ugp <- AromaUgpFile$byChipType("GenomeWideSNP_6,Full", tags="na24,HB20080214");
print(ugp);

then:

ugp <- AromaUgpFile$byChipType("GenomeWideSNP_6,Full", tags="na24");
print(ugp);

then:

ugp <- AromaUgpFile$byChipType("GenomeWideSNP_6,Full");
print(ugp);

If these don't work, add verbose=-100 to the call and see what is reported.

If the above works, we know that the file is working and can be found
by regular means.  Then, try to do:

cdf <- AffymetrixCdfFile$fromChipType("GenomeWideSNP_6", tags="Full");
gi <- getGenomeInformation(cdf, verbose=-100);
